plan.contextChunk: This figure is a potential energy curve for a pair of hydrogen atoms, drawn on a pale blue field with small green spheres added to show the atomic arrangement at three points along it. A tall gradient arrow at the far left, shaded from cream to orange and labeled Energy, gives the sense of the vertical scale, while the plot's own vertical axis is marked only with a plus sign, a 0, and a minus sign, with a horizontal dashed line drawn across at zero. The horizontal axis is labeled Internuclear distance and ends in a magenta arrow pointing right. One magenta curve drops steeply from the upper left, crosses below zero, reaches a rounded minimum, then rises gradually and levels off toward the zero line at large separation. At the top of the steep branch two green spheres overlap, annotated HH (too close). At the right, two widely separated spheres sit above a magenta dashed line joining the letters H and H, annotated H - - - H (too far). At the bottom of the well two just-touching spheres are labeled H-H, and a short vertical dashed line drops from the minimum to the axis, tagged 74 pm, with a green arrow labeled Bond length pointing to it. The depth and position of the single minimum, read against the two extremes flanking it, mark the separation at which attraction and nuclear repulsion balance and fix the length of a covalent bond.

interactions.label: Internuclear distance (pm)
interactions.teaches: Dragging the atoms closer or farther apart moves a point along the energy curve: energy shoots up when nuclei get too close, bottoms out at 74 pm, and climbs back toward zero as the atoms separate — so the bond length is the separation of lowest energy

Clicking the repulsive wall, the well, or the far tail highlights the matching atom sketch and reveals why that region behaves as it does: nuclear repulsion dominates at short range, attraction wins in the well, and the atoms no longer interact when far apart

demo_steps.title: The energy well
demo_steps.narration: The curve starts at its minimum: two H atoms 74 pm apart sit at the lowest energy, with the spheres just touching. This balance of attraction and repulsion is the covalent bond.

demo_steps.title: Push the atoms together
demo_steps.narration: Drag the slider left: the atoms overlap and the energy climbs the steep repulsive wall — 'HH (too close)'. Nuclear repulsion makes very short distances strongly unfavorable.

demo_steps.title: Pull the atoms apart
demo_steps.narration: Drag the slider right: the atoms separate, the energy rises back toward the zero dashed line, and the sketch shows 'H - - - H (too far)' — beyond a certain distance the atoms behave as if unbound.

demo_steps.title: Find the minimum again
demo_steps.narration: Return to 74 pm: the single lowest point on the curve, marked by the green 'Bond length' arrow, is the separation nature settles on for an H–H bond.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: A covalent bond's length is not arbitrary — it is the internuclear distance where the energy curve bottoms out, because that is where attraction and nuclear repulsion exactly balance.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Pale blue plot field with no gridlines. The energy 'axis' is symbolic only: a plus sign above the dashed zero line and a minus below it, with a tall cream-to-orange gradient arrow labeled 'Energy' standing outside the plot at far left. The magenta curve should look Morse-like: near-vertical drop on the left, smooth rounded minimum below zero around x≈74 pm, then a long gently rising asymptote to the dashed zero line. Three green-sphere vignettes placed near the corresponding parts of the curve: overlapping spheres top-left ('HH (too close)'), touching spheres at the well ('H—H'), widely spaced spheres with magenta dashed connector at right ('H - - - H (too far)'). Green 'Bond length' arrow and '74 pm' label in green text anchor the minimum. A draggable marker on the curve and a movable atom pair should track the slider value; clicked regions highlight with a glow on the matching vignette.

authoredContext:
How close are the two nuclei in the H2 molecule? If they are too close, they will repel each other because both are positively charged. Yet if they’re too far apart, they won’t be able to share the bonding electrons. Thus, there is an optimum distance between nuclei that leads to maximum stability (the figure). Called the bond length, this distance is 74 pm in the H–H molecule. Every covalent bond has both a characteristic bond strength and bond length.

A plot of energy versus internuclear distance for two hydrogen atoms. The distance between nuclei at the minimum energy point is the bond length.

A graph of energy versus internuclear distance. A horizontal line separates the positive and negative energy and a curve with a single trough at 74 ppm is shown.
